input.question: Why are some Roman names anglicized to drop their us at the end (Hadrianus to Hadrian) while others were not? Why do we have an Emperor Marcus and not an Emperor Tit or August?
input.ground_truth: Followup question, my last name is August and I can trace myself back to Lithuania as "Augustinavicious" (anglicized). Would there be any connections between Augustus and Augustinavicious? My personal guess is "august" being a loanword, but I'm amazed it made it's way to Lithuania.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why are some Roman names anglicized to drop their us at the end (Hadrianus to Hadrian) while others were not? Why do we have an Emperor Marcus and not an Emperor Tit or August?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Let’s imagine Roman names are like toys. Some toys have a little tag at the end, like “blockus” (that’s just pretend!). When people in England wanted to say these toy names, they sometimes cut off the little tag “us” at the end and just said “block” instead of “blockus.” That’s why Hadrianus becomes Hadrian.

But sometimes, people liked the name the way it was, or it sounded better without changing it, so they didn’t cut off the tag. That’s why we still have names like Marcus.

Also, some Roman names are special and short, like “Titus” or “Augustus.” But when we talk about emperors, we usually use their full or most common names, like “Emperor Marcus” (that’s Marcus Aurelius) or “Emperor Titus.” We don’t usually call them just “Tit” or “August” because those are parts of longer names or titles.

So, some names got shorter because people changed them to make them easier to say, and some names stayed the same because they sounded good or were important. And we use the whole name or the most common version when talking about emperors!
